questions.q: What is a "shard" in the context of a training dataset?
options: A single training sample stored as its own object
A fixed-size bundle of many samples, commonly packed into a tar file and read sequentially
A checkpoint of model weights split across GPUs
A partition of the GPU's memory reserved for data loading
questions.explain: A shard packs hundreds or thousands of samples into one file, so reading it is one sequential, streamable request instead of many tiny ones.

questions.q: What problem does the WebDataset tar-shard pattern specifically solve?
options: It reduces the model's parameter count
It replaces the per-sample request overhead of small-object storage with sequential, streamable reads
It eliminates the need for data shuffling
It compresses model checkpoints for faster upload to S3
questions.explain: By packing many samples into one archive and streaming through it, WebDataset avoids turning every sample into its own storage request.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend that shard count significantly outnumber the total worker count across the cluster?
options: More shards always means better model accuracy
So that workers have spare shards to move to and don't stall waiting for one slow shard to finish
Because S3 requires at least one shard per GPU
To make the dataset smaller on disk
questions.explain: With too few, oversized shards relative to worker count, some workers end up idle waiting for a shard to finish streaming with no next one ready.

questions.q: Why doesn't true random-access shuffling work well for a multi-terabyte corpus in object storage?
options: Random access is actually faster than sequential reads on object storage
Jumping to arbitrary offsets across streaming object storage is inefficient compared to sequential reads
Object storage doesn't support any form of randomization
Random access would exceed the GPU's memory capacity
questions.explain: Object storage is optimized for sequential, streamable access; true random-access shuffling at scale conflicts with that, so shard-level and in-buffer shuffling approximate it instead.

questions.q: In WebDataset's two-level shuffling, what does the in-memory shuffle buffer (e.g. `.shuffle(5000)`) do?
options: It randomizes which shard a worker reads next
It permanently reorders the shard files on disk
It randomizes sample order within a sliding window as a shard streams past
It deletes samples that have already been seen
questions.explain: The in-memory buffer holds a sliding window of samples and emits them in randomized order, approximating randomness without requiring random-access reads.
